questions.question:
Study this HTTP/1.1 persistent connection flow versus HTTP/2 multiplexing. A page needs 6 sub-resources. What is the key problem HTTP/1.1 suffers from that HTTP/2 solves?

HTTP/1.1: GET /a → wait for response → GET /b → wait → GET /c ...
HTTP/2:   Streams 1,3,5,7,9,11 sent simultaneously over ONE TCP connection

values: Connection 1: GET /style.css → wait → GET /app.js → wait → GET /logo.png
Problem: head-of-line blocking — each request waits for prior to complete
HTTP/2 — multiple streams over ONE TCP connection simultaneously:
Stream 3: GET /app.js     ─┤ all in flight at once
No head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer

options: HTTP/1.1 uses UDP; HTTP/2 uses TCP — the protocol change eliminates blocking
HTTP/1.1 suffers from head-of-line blocking — each request on a connection must wait for the prior response; HTTP/2 multiplexes multiple streams over one TCP connection simultaneously
HTTP/1.1 cannot handle more than 2 connections; HTTP/2 allows unlimited connections
HTTP/1.1 sends headers in plain text; HTTP/2 compresses them with gzip
questions.answer: HTTP/1.1 suffers from head-of-line blocking — each request on a connection must wait for the prior response; HTTP/2 multiplexes multiple streams over one TCP connection simultaneously

questions.question:
Scenario:
A developer inspects this HTTP response. What does the ETag header enable, and what request header does the browser send on the NEXT visit to validate the cache?

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
ETag: "33a64df5"
Cache-Control: no-cache
Content-Type: application/json
options: ETag is a version number for API versioning; the browser sends API-Version on the next visit
ETag is a fingerprint of the response content; on the next visit the browser sends If-None-Match: "33a64df5" — if content is unchanged the server responds 304 Not Modified, avoiding retransmission
ETag enables server push; the browser sends Push-Control on the next visit
ETag is only used with POST requests; GET requests use Last-Modified instead
questions.answer: ETag is a fingerprint of the response content; on the next visit the browser sends If-None-Match: "33a64df5" — if content is unchanged the server responds 304 Not Modified, avoiding retransmission

HttpOnly cookies expire when the browser closes; regular cookies persist indefinitely
questions.answer: HttpOnly cookies cannot be accessed or modified by JavaScript (document.cookie); this mitigates XSS attacks that attempt to steal session tokens via script injection

questions.question:
Scenario:
A developer builds a real-time chat feature in a MERN app. Study this flow and identify why WebSocket is used instead of repeated AJAX polling.

diagramData.representation: WebSocket vs AJAX Polling for Real-Time Chat
values: Client: GET /messages every 2 seconds → Server responds → repeat
Problem: wasteful — most responses return no new data; high latency; server load
Step 1: HTTP GET /chat with Upgrade: websocket header
Step 2: Server 101 Switching Protocols → persistent bidirectional channel open
Step 3: Server pushes new messages instantly when they arrive
Step 4: Client sends messages directly over the open connection
Benefit: low latency, no polling, full-duplex, single persistent connection

options: AJAX polling and WebSocket are equivalent — WebSocket is just newer syntax for the same thing

WebSocket establishes a persistent full-duplex connection after an HTTP upgrade handshake; the server can push data instantly to clients without repeated requests — eliminating the latency, server load, and wasted bandwidth of AJAX polling
WebSocket requires a completely different server — it cannot run alongside Express
AJAX polling is preferred for chat because WebSocket connections expire every 30 seconds
questions.answer: WebSocket establishes a persistent full-duplex connection after an HTTP upgrade handshake; the server can push data instantly to clients without repeated requests — eliminating the latency, server load, and wasted bandwidth of AJAX polling
